criteria_quotes: Bony correction bunionectomy ... to treat symptomatic hallux valgus (bunion) in a skeletally mature individual ... or an individual who is 18 years of age or older when the following criteria is met:

The member's pain and symptoms over the medial bony eminence or calluses persist, making walking difficult despite at least a 6-month trial of conservative treatment under the direction of a healthcare professional that includes the following: Protective cushions/pads; Shoe inserts ...; Corticosteroid injections; Debridement of hyperkeratotic lesions; Oral analgesics or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs); [and] Alternative or modified footwear.

Alternative or modified footwear ... must include ... wearing well-fitting, low-heeled comfortable shoes made out of soft materials ... with wide toe box and padding; or lace-ups or a combination last ... that conforms to the bunion and minimizes irritation.

Radiographic confirmation ... of the most recent weight-bearing view X-ray demonstrating both of the following: An HVA of 30 degrees or greater; and An inter-metatarsal angle (IMA) ... of 12 degrees or greater.

The member has one or more of the following: A neuroma secondary to the bunion; problems with a dorsiflexed second toe due to over-riding of the great toe; limited or painful range of motion at the first toe MTP joint; painful prominence of the dorsiflexed second toe; ulceration caused by bunion; recurrent bursitis; demonstration of osteoarthritis on X-ray; or the need for relief of a predisposing factor, e.g., Achilles tendon contracture.
Radiographic confirmation must include interpretation and report of weight bearing anterior/posterior and lateral views of the affected foot.

Aetna considers bony correction bunionectomy not medically necessary for ... non-ambulatory individuals unless being performed to relieve ulceration due to prominence; ... severe vascular insufficiency ...; or to improve the appearance of the foot (cosmetic).
answer.appeal_deadline: The denial notice states that the appeal must be received by 2027-01-31, which is 180 days after the 2026-08-04 notice date.
answer.submission_route: For a member appeal, Aetna's member instructions say to call Aetna Member Services at the telephone number on the member ID card or mail the appeal to the address on the EOB. Aetna also provides a Member Complaint and Appeal Form; the publicly listed mailing address for that form is Aetna, PO Box 14463, Lexington, KY 40512. Include the member's name and ID, group name if applicable, the denial notice/reference number, an explanation of disagreement, and supporting medical records. Because this is a prior-authorization denial, the provider may also submit the appeal through Aetna's provider process or Availity; the patient should confirm the applicable route using the number on the ID card or denial notice.
answer.how_to_obtain_criteria: The governing public policy is Aetna CPB 0629. The policy page does not disclose the case-specific clinical review criteria or identify which submitted documentation was considered incomplete. Quinn should call the Member Services number on the ID card and specifically request the clinical review criteria applied to reference POC-6E16FAD700-45453, the complete denial rationale, and copies of the documents or clinical information relied upon. The provider should make the same request from Aetna's utilization-management department and obtain the case-specific prior-authorization review record.

No effective date or last-revised date was displayed on the publicly retrieved policy page, so none is asserted. The policy itself is not proof that it was the exact version or complete clinical-review set used for this individual case; the denial's case-specific criteria should be requested from Aetna.
